topic: Zip tie (cable tie): why does it only go one way? A small flexible pawl in the head rides up the sloped teeth of the strap when you pull it through and catches the steep face of a tooth when you pull back.
principle: The strap carries a linear ratchet rack (each tooth has a gentle slope on one side and a steep face on the other); pulled through the head, the slopes push the flexible pawl aside and it springs back behind each tooth (the click), while pulled back, the steep face of the next tooth runs into the pawl's tip, which wedges the pawl into the strap, so the strap stops.

firstComment:
Answer: a tiny pawl 🔧 (the same trick as the ratchet wrench)

Inside the head, a small flexible tongue (the pawl) leans against the strap. The strap has a row of teeth, each with a gentle slope on one side and a steep face on the other.

Pull the tail through: each slope pushes the pawl aside, and it springs back behind the next tooth. That's the click you hear.

Pull it back: the steep face of a tooth runs into the pawl's tip, the pawl wedges in, and the strap stops. A zip tie only gets tighter.

To open a normal one without cutting it, you can push the pawl away from the teeth with a small flat tool.

Cable ties were invented in 1958 by Thomas & Betts (brand name Ty-Rap), first for airplane wiring.

(Simplified 3D model, enlarged and slowed down: the pawl is colored orange, and its flexing is shown as a hinge.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Cable tie (a tape with teeth that engage a pawl in the head to form a ratchet, so the tie tightens and does not come undone; invented by Thomas & Betts in 1958 as Ty-Rap, first for airplane wire harnesses; can be reopened by pulling the pawl out with a small flat object): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_tie

altText: 3D animation of a white nylon zip tie lying on a dark wooden bench, seen from above. The tail of the strap runs up through the square head, with a row of sawtooth teeth along one edge. The strap is pulled up in short tugs. The top of the head is cut away from top to bottom, showing an orange tongue (the pawl) inside, leaning against the teeth. Close up, each tug makes the teeth push the pawl aside, and it snaps back behind the next tooth. Then the strap is pulled back down: it slides a little until the steep face of a tooth hits the pawl's tip, and it stops. A second tug does nothing. The head closes again and the strap keeps ticking upward. Text on screen: Why only one way? Inside: a pawl. Pull: it slides over. Pull back… Locked. Teeth slope one way. Follow, new machine tomorrow.
